slides.title: The goal: predict the next token
slides.summary: Pretraining teaches the model one thing: predicting the next token of real text, on a huge scale.
body: Pretraining has one simple goal: take a piece of real text and, at every point, guess the token that comes next.

No one needs to label anything, because the text contains its own answers. The input is the text, and the answer is the same text moved along by one token. This is called self-supervised learning, and it's why training can use trillions of tokens from web pages, books and code.
Thanks to the causal mask, one pass over a 4,096-token text gives 4,096 guesses to learn from at once. On the right, one short sentence becomes four training examples.

body.note: Predicting the next token sounds simple, but doing it well takes a lot: grammar, facts, reasoning, a writer's style, how code works. The model learns all of that along the way, just by getting better at this one task.

code: inputs, targets = ids[:-1], ids[1:]     # shift by one

blocks.html: One sequence, four predictions, one pass.

slides.title: Measuring mistakes: cross-entropy loss
slides.summary: The loss measures how surprised the model was by the right answer. Training tries to make that surprise smaller.
body: To learn, the model needs one number that says how wrong it was. At each position, take the probability it gave to the token that actually came next, and compute loss = −log p(correct). Then average over all positions. This is called cross-entropy loss.

ul: The right token got 90%: loss 0.11. Small.
The right token got 1%: loss 4.6. Big.
The right token got 0.01%: loss 9.2. Huge. <mark>Being confidently wrong is punished the most.</mark>

body: For comparison: random guessing between 50,000 tokens scores ln(50,000) ≈ 10.8. Well-trained models get to about 2 or lower on typical web text.
Perplexity is e^loss. Think of it as how many tokens the model is stuck choosing between, on average. A loss of 2 means a perplexity of about 7.4, as if picking from seven equally likely options.
Drag the slider to see how loss and perplexity respond.

slides.title: How the model learns: backprop and gradient descent
slides.summary: Training nudges every weight a tiny step, over and over, in whichever direction lowers the loss.
body: Once we have the loss, we need to know how to change each weight to lower it. Backpropagation works that out. For every weight, it finds the gradient: if this weight goes up a little, does the loss go up or down, and by how much?
It uses the chain rule from calculus, working backwards through every step of the model. You never write it yourself; tools like PyTorch do it automatically.
Gradient descent then moves every weight a small step downhill: w ← w − lr · gradient. This is repeated millions of times.
The size of each step, the learning rate (lr), is the most important setting:

ul: Too small: training is very slow. Try 0.1.
About right: it quickly settles at the bottom. Try 0.5.
Too big: each step goes too far, bouncing from side to side or shooting off completely. Try 0.9, then 1.05.

body.note: Imagine walking down a hill in thick fog, feeling the slope under your feet. You can't see the valley, but stepping downhill each time gets you there, as long as your steps aren't so big that you jump right over it.

code: loss.backward()                  # fills p.grad for every weight
p -= lr * p.grad         # real code: optimizer.step()

slides.title: The real training loop
slides.summary: Real training is the same loop, plus engineering to keep it fast and stable across thousands of GPUs.
body: The basic loop stays the same: run the model, measure the loss, backpropagate, update. But with billions of parameters and trillions of tokens, it needs extra help:

ul: AdamW optimiser: instead of one step size for everything, it adjusts the step for each weight based on its recent gradients (momentum). It also slowly shrinks weights over time (weight decay), which helps the model handle new text well.
Learning-rate schedule: start with tiny steps and build up (warm-up), then slowly make them smaller, often along a cosine curve, so training settles down.
Mixed precision: do most of the maths with 16-bit numbers (bf16) for speed, while keeping a 32-bit copy of the weights for accuracy.

Parallelism: the model and everything training keeps track of are far too big for one GPU. So the work is split up in several ways at once: different data on different GPUs, each big matrix split across GPUs, different layers on different GPUs, and for MoE models, different experts on different GPUs.
Gradient clipping: if a gradient is suddenly huge (a loss spike), shrink it so one bad batch can't ruin the model.

body: The curve on the right has the usual shape: a steep drop as the model learns the easy patterns, then a long, slow climb towards better.

body.note: Scaling laws: loss goes down smoothly and predictably as you add more parameters, data and computing. Because it's so predictable, AI companies are willing to spend huge sums on a single training run.

slides.title: From text predictor to assistant
slides.summary: A base model only continues text. More training stages turn it into a helpful assistant.
body: Pretraining produces a base model. It's amazing at continuing text, but it isn't an assistant. Ask it a question and it might reply with three more questions, as if it were continuing a list of exam questions.
Three more stages, together called post-training, turn it into an assistant:

ul: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): train on example chats, written or picked to show good assistant behaviour, in the chat template. It's the same next-token loss, usually counted only on the assistant's replies. The model learns the format and its role.

Preference tuning: show pairs of answers where one was judged better, and push the model towards the better kind. RLHF uses human rankings to train a scoring model, then improves the assistant with reinforcement learning. RLAIF uses feedback from an AI instead, for example judging answers against a written set of principles, as in Anthropic's Constitutional AI. DPO skips the scoring model and learns from the pairs directly.

Reinforcement learning on checkable tasks: reward the model when it gets an answer right that can be checked, like a maths result or code that passes its tests. This has driven much of the recent progress in reasoning models.

body.note: Post-training uses only a small part of the computing that pretraining does, but it changes behaviour hugely. <mark>Pretraining provides the knowledge; post-training shapes how it's used.</mark>

body: The Assistant architecture section showed what happens next: how the trained model is wrapped in a full assistant system.
Reinforcement learning on checkable tasks is also what creates Reasoning models, the next chapter. After that, Why LLMs hallucinate covers one of the best-known problems with these models.

blocks.html: Pretraining uses by far the most computing. The later stages are small in comparison, but change behaviour hugely.
